title: Burden and Changes in Quality of Life among Patients Undergoing Intravitreal Drug Administration (IVOM) for Exudative Age-Related Macular Degeneration, Diabetic Retinopathy, Secondary Macular Edema Following Retinal Vein Occlusion, and Secondary Myopic Choroidal Neovascularization
summary:
Retinal diseases, including neovascular age-related macular degeneration
(nAMD), diabetic macular edema (DME), macular edema resulting from retinal
venous occlusions (RVO), and myopic choroidal neovascularization (mCNV),
are major contributors to visual impairment and blindness in Western countries
and significantly impact patients’ quality of life (QoL). The primary therapeutic approach for preserving visual function involves the intravitreal administration of anti-VEGF (vascular endothelial growth factor) agents, whose efficacy and safety have been extensively demonstrated previously.
PROMs (“Patient-Reported Outcome Measures”), including questionnaires to
assess quality of life, are valuable tools for evaluating the
burden of disease. As previously demonstrated, patients who experienced an
improvement in visual acuity after the start of therapy reported significantly better scores on standardized questionnaires assessing vision-related quality of life (vrQoL),
while patients who experienced a deterioration in visual acuity
showed a decline in quality of life. In addition, there are already indications of other potential treatment-related factors that could influence quality of life during treatment, including baseline visual acuity, injection frequency, and
overall health status. The need for mostly continuous
IVOM therapy to maintain visual acuity places a significant burden on patients,
particularly due to challenges such as frequent clinic visits, the
psychological strain of living with a chronic condition, and
potential financial burdens, such as the cost of regular taxi rides
for doctor’s appointments. It has also been reported that a significant proportion of
IVOM patients require support from family members and experience anxiety
related to their diagnosis during the course of treatment.
Negative changes in patient satisfaction over the course of therapy pose a
risk of treatment delays, undertreatment, or treatment discontinuation, which
in turn is associated with a poor prognosis. A better understanding of patient-reported quality of life, as well as of factors associated with changes in it, could help in the future to provide patients with more targeted counseling as part of IVOM therapy and improve care
overall. With our study, we plan to conduct an ambispective clinical
investigation to assess longitudinal changes in QoL and
anxiety symptoms, as well as associated treatment factors, in a patient cohort that
is receiving IVOM therapy as part of routine clinical care.
The study aims to investigate both general and treatment-related
factors associated with changes in patients’ QoL and anxiety symptoms
in order to identify overarching, underlying problem areas among
IVOM patients undergoing treatment. A longitudinal
comparison between the various patient groups with different
diagnoses is also planned, as well as a comparison between patients
with a short treatment history to date (treatment-naive or < 24 months since
the start of IVOM therapy) and those with a longer-standing
treatment history (> 24 months), in order to identify subgroups that are
particularly severely affected.

Study Design: A monocenter, ambispective study without randomization and without
blinding.
Study Procedure: Participants are asked to complete the questionnaires provided at
the three scheduled study time points, with the time required per
assessment time point (baseline/study enrollment; 12 months later; 24 months
later) is approximately 20 minutes. As part of a retrospective data collection,
the course of treatment up to the time of enrollment in the
study will also be recorded based on routine outpatient consultations previously conducted at the clinic. The subsequent course of treatment between the
study time points, which also takes place during clinical outpatient consultations, will be recorded prospectively starting at the beginning of the study. No
additional examinations or visits will be conducted as part of the
planned study. The questionnaires are completed by the patients,
with the assistance of a family member if necessary, at the clinic while waiting
for their clinic appointment or, alternatively, at home. The completed questionnaires
are then returned to the study management team.
Pseudonymized data are entered and analyzed using Excel and SPSS.
Data sources/data to be collected:
• Medical records (recording of treatment duration at baseline, unilateral or
bilateral involvement, baseline visual acuity of the affected eye and the
contralateral eye, visual acuity after 12 or 24 months, number of IVOM
injections at baseline, number of
IVOM consultation appointments over 12 or 24 months, as well as the number of IVOM
injections administered and medications used, complications and side effects of
IVOM therapy, other ocular diseases, patient age, gender, place of residence
(to calculate travel distance in kilometers)
• Questionnaires (EQ-5D-5L), NEI-VFQ-25, GAD-7, BFI-10, general
questionnaire on pre-existing conditions, social situation, integration, and mobility)
Planned timeline/planned study duration:
48 months (24-month recruitment phase, 12-month follow-up survey, 24-month follow-up survey).

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Inclusion Criteria:
-Patients diagnosed with (study eye):
• Exudative age-related macular degeneration (H35.30)
• Macular edema associated with diabetic retinopathy (H36.0)
• Macular edema associated with venous occlusion (H34.8; H34.2)
• Secondary choroidal neovascularization associated with myopia (H31.8)
-Sufficient knowledge of German to complete the questionnaires
-The patient has given consent to participate in the study, and a signed informed consent form is on file before any study-related procedures are performed.
Exclusion criteria:
Exclusion Criteria:
- Presence of other relevant ophthalmic conditions that could influence the assessment of the study endpoints, including:
• Presence of other retinal diseases (e.g., central serous chorioretinopathy)
• Glaucoma
• Ocular surface disease (e.g., corneal scarring, severe dry eye symptoms associated with Sjögren’s syndrome)
• Active or recurrent ocular inflammation (e.g., clinically significant blepharitis, conjunctivitis, scleritis, keratitis, or uveitis)
-History of photodynamic therapy
